opus-5.5.text:
Well, if you look at the history of AI failures, and I've been collecting them for years, there's a very clear pattern. The damage is proportional to the capability and the scope of the system. Early on you had narrow systems making narrow mistakes: a spell checker suggests the wrong word, a recommendation engine shows you a bad movie. Annoying, but the damage is contained to that domain.

As systems became more capable and were deployed more widely, the failures got bigger. You saw trading algorithms causing flash crashes, wiping out billions in minutes. You saw biased systems affecting millions of people in hiring, lending, criminal justice. The failure is still local in some sense, but the reach is much larger.

Now we're moving toward general systems, systems that operate across every domain and are connected to everything: financial systems, infrastructure, communication, potentially weapons and biology. Once a system is capable of affecting all of humanity, a failure is no longer a bug you patch in the next release. It could be the last mistake we get to make. With existential risk, there's no learning from experience, no second iteration.

What worries me most is that the standard approach in cybersecurity or software engineering is that you accept some failure rate. You find vulnerabilities, you fix them, you get better over time. That works when failures are recoverable. With superintelligent systems, you need essentially zero failures over potentially billions of decisions, indefinitely, against an adversary smarter than you. I don't think that's achievable with current methods, and I'm not sure it's achievable in principle. That's the core problem: the stakes are scaling to infinity while our ability to verify and control these systems is not scaling at all.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says that damage is proportional to a system’s capability and scope.

fable-5.1.text:
So, I think the simplest way to see it is to look at the history of AI failures. I actually keep a list, a kind of catalog of AI accidents, and if you look at it, the pattern is very clear. Early systems failed in small ways. A spam filter misclassifies an email. A spell checker suggests the wrong word. The damage is local, it's annoying, it's recoverable. Then systems get more capable, they get deployed more widely, and the failures scale with that. A self-driving car kills a pedestrian. A trading algorithm wipes out a lot of money in a few minutes. A recommendation system influences what millions of people believe. In every case, the damage is proportional to the capability and the reach of the system.

And the frightening thing is that this is a pretty consistent trend. Every single system we've built has failed at some point. I don't know of any exception. So if we extrapolate, and we're talking about superintelligent systems, systems that are more capable than all of humanity combined, systems that are making decisions about infrastructure, about economy, about biology, then the failure of such a system is not a local failure anymore. It's not one person who dies, it's not one company that loses money. It's potentially everyone, everywhere, at the same time. That's why I talk about existential risk. The scale of harm goes from individual, to group, to civilization, and finally to the whole of humanity, and at that last level you don't get a second chance.

What's different about that level is that we lose our usual safety mechanism, which is learning from mistakes. Everything we know about engineering, about safety, comes from trial and error. We build a bridge, it collapses, we learn and build a better bridge. With existential risk there is no learning from the error, because there's no one left to learn. So you have to get it right the first time, and we have never done that with any complex software. Our track record is bugs, patches, bugs again. I don't see why it would suddenly be different for the most complex system ever created.

And I would also say it's not just about death or physical destruction. There are failures that are permanent in other ways. You could lose control of your future, you could end up in a world where humans are no longer the decision makers, and that's irreversible even if everyone is technically alive. So when I think about damage scaling, I think about both the magnitude, how many people are affected, and the reversibility, whether you can ever fix it. With narrow AI, both were small. With general or superintelligent AI, both go to the maximum. That's the problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says that as systems become more capable, their failures scale, and that damage is proportional to the system’s capability.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that the consequences scale with the system’s ability to act. If an AI makes a mistake in a game, you lose a game. If it’s driving a car, somebody can die. Those are serious failures, but they’re relatively local. When you have systems making decisions across critical infrastructure, economies, or military operations, the same kind of failure can affect millions or billions of people.

And those failures may be correlated. If everyone relies on the same system, one mistake can propagate everywhere. You don’t necessarily have independent failures that other people can contain.

At the extreme, you’re talking about an existential catastrophe—human extinction, or humanity permanently losing control over its future. That doesn’t mean every advanced system will cause that outcome. It means that as capability and autonomy increase, the worst possible failure becomes something we cannot recover from. We can’t rely on learning from that mistake afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says consequences scale with an AI system’s ability to act and affect people, illustrating how failures become more damaging as systems operate across larger domains.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that the scale of the damage grows with the capability of the system and the scope of its access. A narrow system fails, and perhaps you lose money or get a bad recommendation. A system controlling critical infrastructure, conducting scientific research, or making military decisions can fail in ways that affect millions or billions of people.

And those failures may be correlated. If everyone relies on the same system, one mistake can propagate everywhere. You don’t necessarily have independent failures that we can recover from one at a time.

At the extreme, we’re talking about a failure that humanity cannot recover from. That changes the safety question. It’s no longer just, ‘How often does this system make mistakes?’ It’s, ‘Can one mistake be catastrophic, and do we have a meaningful way to stop it?’

r001.rationale: The response states that damage grows with a system’s capability, directly conveying the criterion’s scaling relationship.
